doc_description: Corning Incorporated’s 2021 Form 10‑K (GLW) details its global five‑segment materials‑science businesses (display glass, optical fiber/connectivity, specialty materials including Gorilla Glass, environmental substrates/filters, and life sciences), reports $14.1B in sales with growth across all segments, reflects full‑year consolidation of Hemlock Semiconductor, and highlights capital actions including Samsung Display’s preferred conversion and a $1.5B share repurchase, alongside extensive risk, IP, and human‑capital disclosures.

nodes.summary:
- Part of Corning Incorporated’s annual report (Part I, Item 1. Business) with a forward-looking statements caution referencing Risk Factors and MD&A.
- Company overview: origins in 1851; incorporated in NY in 1936; name changed to Corning Incorporated in 1989. Leader in materials science leveraging glass science, ceramic science, and optical physics; success driven by R&D, material/process innovation, and deep customer relationships.
- Markets served: optical communications, mobile consumer electronics, display technology, automotive emissions control, laboratory products, and other glass products.
- Representative products: damage-resistant cover glass; precision display glass; optical fiber, cable, wireless and connectivity solutions; life-sciences tools; and clean-air technologies.
- Operating structure: five reportable segments—Display Technologies, Optical Communications, Specialty Materials, Environmental Technologies, and Life Sciences; manufacturing at 119 plants in 15 countries.
- Display Technologies segment: produces glass substrates for LCD and OLED displays used in TVs, notebooks, monitors, tablets, and handheld devices; relies on Corning’s proprietary, highly automated fusion manufacturing process delivering pristine surfaces, thermal stability, dimensional uniformity, scalability, and cost-effectiveness.
- Recent display innovations: EAGLE XG Slim Glass (>35 billion square feet sold); Astra Glass for high-resolution/oxide backplanes; Lotus NXT Glass for high-temperature processing and flexible/small devices; first Gen 10/10.5 substrate sizes for large displays.
- Display footprint and IP: manufacturing in China, South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan; patent protection and trade secrets are important; segment was 26% of 2021 consolidated net sales.
- Optical Communications segment: Corning pioneered low-loss optical fiber (1970); addresses growing bandwidth demand and migration from copper to optical; delivers solutions across the network edge.
- Segment organization: carrier network (telecom infrastructure for video/data/voice) and enterprise network (optical networks for businesses, governments, individuals).
- Carrier network portfolio: broad fibers (Vascade for submarine; LEAF for long-haul/metro; SMF-28 ULL/TXF, SMF-28e+, ClearCurve, SMF-28 Ultra/Contour for various applications), sold directly and via third-party cablers; cable lines (RocketRibbon, miniXtend) for outdoor/indoor and 5G deployments.
- Connectivity and systems: hardware and equipment (assemblies, hardware, connectors, components, closures, network interface devices) offered as components or integrated solutions, including Evolv (pre-connectorized FTTH/5G) and Centrix (high-density fiber management).

nodes.title: Optical Communications Segment
nodes.heading: Optical Communications Segment
nodes.start_phrase:
Corning invented the world’s firs
t low-loss optical fiber in 1970.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Corning’s business segments and product leadership, focusing on Display Technologies, Optical Communications, and Specialty Materials.
- Display Technologies: Positions Corning as a leader in precision glass for larger, thinner, flexible, high‑resolution displays; highlights key innovations (EAGLE XG Slim Glass, Astra Glass for oxide backplanes and LTPS processes, Lotus NXT for high‑temperature/small and flexible devices, and first Gen 10/10.5 substrate sizes for large displays). Notes manufacturing footprint across China, South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan; emphasizes patent/trade secret importance; segment accounted for 26% of 2021 net sales.
- Optical Communications: Traces heritage from inventing low‑loss optical fiber; addresses surging data/video demand driving shift from copper to fiber. Details carrier and enterprise product groupings:
  - Carrier network: Broad fiber portfolio (Vascade for submarine, LEAF for long‑haul/metro, SMF‑28 ULL/TXF, SMF‑28e+, ClearCurve, SMF‑28 Ultra/Contour), internal and external cabling (RocketRibbon, miniXtend) for outdoor/indoor and 5G; hardware/equipment (assemblies, connectors, closures, components) and integrated solutions (Evolv for pre‑connectorized FTTH/5G, Centrix for high‑density fiber management); includes select copper products (subscriber demarcation, xDSL passives, enclosures).
  - Enterprise network: ClearCurve multimode fiber for data centers; hardware/equipment; integrated solutions (EDGE platform for high‑density cabling to 400G+; Everon for indoor cellular connectivity).
  - Manufacturing footprint: Fiber in North Carolina, China, India (Poland added in 2022); cabling in North Carolina, Poland, regional sites; hardware/equipment in Texas, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, Poland, China. Notes extensive patent portfolio and limited royalty income; segment represented 31% of 2021 net sales.
- Specialty Materials: Provides 150+ glass, glass‑ceramic, and crystal formulations plus precision metrology instruments/software for diverse markets (mobile electronics, semiconductor optics/consumables, aerospace/defense optics, radiation shielding, sunglasses, telecom components).
  - Gorilla Glass (including Gorilla Glass Victus) for enhanced drop/scratch resistance, optical clarity, touch sensitivity, RF transparency; manufactured in the U.S., South Korea, Taiwan.
  - Ceramic Shield: First transparent, color‑free glass‑ceramic for smartphones, co‑developed and scaled with Apple for iPhone front covers.
  - Semiconductor optics: HPFS Fused Silica, ULE Ultra‑Low Expansion Glass, metrology instruments, custom assemblies; manufactured in New York.
  - Ultra‑flat/ultra‑thin glass wafers/substrates for AR, advanced packaging, 3D sensing; made in New York, France, China.
  - Additional products: Tinted sunglasses and radiation shielding produced in France.
- Emphasis on intellectual property across segments, referencing a broader “Patents and Trademarks” section.

nodes.title: Specialty Materials Segment
nodes.heading: Specialty Materials Segment
nodes.start_phrase:
The Specialty Materia
ls segment manufactures products that provide more than 150 material formulations for glass, glass ceramics, and crystals, as well as precisionmetrology instruments and so
ftware to meet requirements for unique customer needs.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Corning business segments with focus on products, technologies, manufacturing footprint, intellectual property, and 2021 sales mix.
- Optical Communications:
  - Portfolio spans optical and select copper-based products: subscriber demarcation, connection/protection devices, xDSL passive solutions, and outside plant enclosures.
  - Enterprise network solutions leveraging optical fiber (e.g., ClearCurve ultra-bendable multimode fiber) for private and hyperscale data centers.
  - Hardware/equipment: cable assemblies, connectors, optical components/couplers, closures; integrated solutions like EDGE (high-density, pre-terminated cabling, path to 400G+) and Everon (indoor cellular connectivity).
  - Manufacturing: fiber in North Carolina, China, India; new Poland fiber facility (2022); cabling in North Carolina, Poland, regional sites; hardware/equipment in Texas, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, Poland, China.
  - Strong patent portfolio; some outbound licensing (non-material royalty income); uses third-party patents.
  - Accounted for 31% of 2021 consolidated net sales.
- Specialty Materials:
  - Produces 150+ material formulations (glass, glass ceramics, crystals) plus precision metrology instruments/software for diverse markets: mobile electronics, semiconductor optics, aerospace/defense, radiation shielding, sunglasses, telecom components.
  - Key products: Gorilla Glass (including Victus), co-developed Ceramic Shield for iPhone; semiconductor optics (HPFS Fused Silica, ULE glass), optical metrology; ultra-flat/thin glass wafers for AR, advanced packaging, 3D sensing.
  - Manufacturing: Gorilla Glass in the U.S., South Korea, Taiwan; semiconductor optics in New York; wafers in New York, France, China; sunglasses/radiation shielding in France.
  - Emphasis on patents and trademarks; growing IP portfolio.
  - Represented 14% of 2021 consolidated net sales.
- Environmental Technologies:
  - Ceramic substrates and filters for global vehicle emissions control; long-standing leadership since the 1970s.
  - Recent products: low-mass FLORA substrates and DuraTrap GC gasoline particulate filters.
  - Manufacturing in New York, Virginia, China, Germany, South Africa.
  - Sells primarily to emission control system manufacturers (specified by OEMs).
  - Extensive patent portfolio; uses certain third-party patents.
  - Contributed 11% of 2021 consolidated net sales.
- Life Sciences:
  - Laboratory products and solutions supporting drug discovery, biologics, vaccines, and cell/gene therapies; focus on improving productivity, efficiency, cost, and timelines.
  - Products: consumables (plastic vessels, liquid handling), specialty surfaces, cell culture media/serum, general labware, equipment.
  - Applications: screening/toxicology, advanced cell culture, genomics, cell manufacturing/bioproduction.
  - Brands: Corning, Falcon, PYREX, Axygen; sold globally via distributors to pharma/biotech, CMOs, central labs, academia, hospitals, government.
  - Manufacturing across multiple U.S. states plus China, France, Mexico, Poland.
  - Importance of patents and brand recognition.
  - Accounted for 9% of 2021 consolidated net sales.

nodes.title: Environmental Technologies Segment
nodes.heading: Environmental Technologies Segment
nodes.start_phrase:
Corning’s Environmental Technolog
ies segment manufactures ceramic substrates and filter products for emissions control in mobile applications around the world.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Corning business segments with emphasis on product focus, customers, manufacturing footprint, intellectual property, and contribution to 2021 consolidated net sales.
- Specialty Materials segment: highlights the importance of patent protection and brand recognition via trademarks; maintains a growing IP portfolio; represented 14% of 2021 consolidated net sales.
- Environmental Technologies segment: produces ceramic substrates and filters for global vehicle emissions control; legacy innovation from the 1970s and recent launches of low-mass Corning FLORA substrates and DuraTrap GC gasoline particulate filters; manufactures in New York, Virginia, China, Germany, and South Africa; sells primarily to catalyzers/emission control system manufacturers per OEM specifications; relies on extensive patents and licensed IP; accounted for 11% of 2021 consolidated net sales.
- Life Sciences segment: long-standing global supplier of lab products supporting research and bioproduction across small molecules, biologics, vaccines, and cell/gene therapies; leverages expertise in materials science, polymer surface science, cell culture, and cell biology; offerings include consumables, specialty surfaces, media/serum, general labware, and equipment for applications like drug discovery, screening, toxicology, advanced cell culture, genomics, and cell manufacturing; primary brands are Corning, Falcon, PYREX, and Axygen; sold globally via distributors to pharma, biotech, CMOs, testing labs, academia, hospitals, and governments; manufactures across multiple U.S. sites and in China, France, Mexico, and Poland; emphasizes patents and trademarks; contributed 9% of 2021 consolidated net sales.

nodes.title: Life Sciences Segment
nodes.heading: Life Sciences Segment
nodes.start_phrase:
As a leading developer, manuf
acturer and global supplier of laboratory products for over 105 years, Corning’s Life Sciences segment works with researchers and drugmanufacturers seeking 
to drive innovation, increase efficiencies, reduce costs and compress timelines.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Corning Incorporated’s business segments, their products, markets, manufacturing footprint, intellectual property importance, 2021 sales contribution, and competitive landscape.

- Specialty Materials (brief mention):
  - Emphasis on patents/trademarks for products, technologies, and processes; brand recognition important.
  - Accounted for 14% of consolidated net sales in 2021.

- Environmental Technologies:
  - Manufactures ceramic substrates and filters for automotive and diesel emissions control; pioneered cellular ceramic substrates for catalytic converters in the 1970s.
  - Recent products include low-mass Corning FLORA substrates and DuraTrap GC gasoline particulate filters.
  - Customers: catalyzers and emissions system manufacturers (usage typically specified by vehicle/engine OEMs).
  - Manufacturing: New York, Virginia, China, Germany, South Africa.
  - Strong patent portfolio and key licenses; IP is critical.
  - Represented 11% of 2021 consolidated net sales.

- Life Sciences:
  - Longstanding supplier of laboratory products supporting small molecule drugs, biologics, vaccines, and cell/gene therapies.
  - Products: consumables (plastic vessels, liquid handling, specialty surfaces), cell culture media/serum, labware, equipment; used from discovery through bioproduction.
  - Brands: Corning, Falcon, PYREX, Axygen.
  - Go-to-market primarily via distributors to pharma/biotech companies, CMOs, testing labs, academia, hospitals, and governments.
  - Manufacturing: multiple U.S. states plus China, France, Mexico, Poland.
  - Patents/trademarks and brand loyalty are important.
  - Contributed 9% of 2021 consolidated net sales.

- All Other:
  - Aggregates businesses below reporting thresholds, including Hemlock Semiconductor Group (consolidated since Sept. 9, 2020), pharmaceutical technologies, auto glass, new product lines, development projects, and certain corporate investments.
  - Represented 9% of 2021 consolidated net sales.
  - References to Notes 3 and 4 for HSG details.

- Competition (overall and by segment):
  - Corning competes with large domestic and foreign manufacturers; seeks advantage via R&D, customer relationships, reliable supply, product quality, service, and technical specification, though no assurance of sustaining advantage.
  - Display Technologies: largest producer of flat panel display glass substrates; advantages from proprietary fusion process and product quality; competitors AGC Inc. and Nippon Electric Glass Co., Ltd.
  - Optical Communications: leadership in carrier and enterprise networks; faces consolidation and pricing pressure; advantages from manufacturing scale, fiber process, technology, and IP; competitors CommScope Inc. and Prysmian Group S.p.A.
  - Specialty Materials: broad materials and optical capabilities serving semiconductor, aerospace, defense, industrial, commercial, and telecom markets; competitors Schott AG, AGC Inc., Nippon Electric Glass, Heraeus.
  - Environmental Technologies: strong position in automotive/diesel substrate and filter markets; advantages in product portfolio, engineering collaboration, service, global presence, and innovation; competitors NGK Insulators, Ltd. and Ibiden Co., Ltd.

- Cross-references: Additional segment and geographic financial information noted in MD&A and Note 20; patents and trademarks discussed under a dedicated section.

ains a strong position in the worldwide market for automotive ceramic substrate and filter products, as well as in the heavy-duty and light-dutydiesel vehicle markets.

- Trade and export controls: Extensive import/export regulations (e.g., CBP, BIS, OAC, DDTC, OFAC and foreign counterparts) create risks of scrutiny, penalties, and restrictions on importing/exporting products or providing services. Future regulatory changes and interpretations are unpredictable.
- Anti-corruption laws: Exposure to the FCPA and similar foreign laws, with heightened global enforcement. International operations—especially in developing countries—increase risk of alleged violations, potentially causing severe sanctions, business disruption, and reputational/financial harm.
- Third-party risks: Reputational and legal risks from partners or customers operating under differing legal and business norms, potentially leading to violations.
- International trade policy impacts: Tariffs, quotas, capital controls, anti-dumping actions, “buy national” policies, regulatory delays, and new barriers to entry could reduce demand, hinder manufacturing/sales abroad, and adversely affect competitiveness, operations, and financial results.

- Equity in earnings of affiliates improved to a $35 gain (from a $25 loss in 2020).

- Net income attributable to Corning was $1,906 (+272%; 14% of net sales).

- Specialty Materials: $2,008 (+7%); strong demand for premium cover materials and advanced optics used in semiconductor manufacturing.

- Life Sciences: $1,234 (+24%); ongoing pandemic-related demand, recovery in research labs, and strong bioproduction/diagnostics consumables.

nodes.title: Valuation of the Previously Held Equity Interest from the Consolidation of HSG

nodes.title: Impairment of assets held for use
nodes.heading: Impairment of assets held for use
nodes.start_phrase: We are required to ass ess the recoverability of the carrying value of long-lived assets when an indicator of impairment has been identified.
nodes.summary:
- Consolidation of HSG and remeasurement: Corning applied the acquisition method to a change in control of HSG, fair-valuing acquired assets (including intangibles, fixed assets, inventories) and liabilities (debt, customer deposits, deferred revenue). Previously held equity interest was remeasured to fair value with resulting gain recognized. Independent appraisals and acceptable valuation models were used; allocation-period adjustments (up to one year) may change values and goodwill.

- September 2020 Redemption details: HSG redeemed DuPont’s interest for $250 million, triggering consolidation and a $498 million pre-tax gain on Corning’s previously held equity method investment, valued via an income approach (16.5% discount rate, 0% terminal growth).

- Intangible assets recognized: $215 million for developed technologies/know-how and $70 million for other intangibles, amortized over ~20 and ~15 years, respectively. Valuation methods included relief-from-royalty ($125 million; 21% discount rate; 7% royalty) and multi-period excess earnings under the income approach ($90 million; 19% discount rate).

- Customer deposits and deferred revenue at consolidation: Recorded a $264 million customer deposit at fair value (discount rates 2.54%–3.23%), repayable 2029–2034 contingent on purchase obligations; and $1,070 million of deferred revenue at fair value using a cost build-up method with a normal profit margin.

- Impairment of long-lived assets: Process for identifying and measuring impairments, including indicators (market price declines, adverse changes in use/legal factors, cost overruns, sustained losses, early disposal). Asset groups are identified at the lowest level of largely independent cash flows, often combined across locations within segments sharing supply chains. Recoverability tests use undiscounted cash flows; if failed, fair value is estimated via an income approach. Assumptions are most sensitive to market growth, volume, and pricing.

- Precious metals in manufacturing equipment: Platinum and rhodium components are not depreciated due to long useful lives; reviewed for impairment across all stages (in-process, reclamation, fabrication). Carrying values were $3.5 billion (2021) and $3.4 billion (2020), both significantly below market value. Future impairment risk exists if Display Technologies or Specialty Materials experience significant demand/profitability declines.

- 2020 impairment charge: $217 million pre-tax impairment and disposal loss within “All Other” due to discontinuation/reprioritization of certain R&D programs; fair value measured with Level 3 inputs.

- Income taxes: Significant judgment in assessing realizability of deferred tax assets and evaluating uncertain tax positions under ASC 740 (more-likely-than-not threshold, recognition limited to amounts probable upon settlement). Estimates can change with new information.

- Fair value measurements: Use of observable and unobservable inputs under the fair value hierarchy and highest-and-best-use for non-financial assets. Major categories measured at fair value include investments, certain pension assets, and derivatives, valued primarily with observable market inputs.

- Derivatives and hedging: Interest rate swaps and FX forwards (yen, won, euro, TWD, yuan, pound). Cash flow hedge changes recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and reclassified when hedged items affect earnings; non-designated contracts recognized in earnings. Credit risk impacts deemed immaterial.

- Litigation and contingencies: Outcome assessments based on counsel, case law, and case-specific factors; other possible liabilities (e.g., tax planning, environmental) require judgment for accrual or disclosure; actual outcomes may require adjustments.

- Cross-references: Notes on investments, HSG transactions and acquisitions, restructuring/impairment, fair value measurements, and the Legal Proceedings section.

nodes.title: Revenue recognition

nodes.start_phrase: The Company recognizes revenue when all performance obligations under the terms of a contract with our customer are satisfied, and control of the product has been transferred to the customer.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risks
structure.heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risks
structure.start_phrase: We operate and conduct busin ess in many foreign countries and as a result are exposed to movements in foreign currency exchange rates.
structure.summary:
- The company operates globally and faces foreign currency exchange risk affecting both earnings from foreign-currency transactions and translation of foreign subsidiaries’ results.
- Primary currency exposures include the Japanese yen, South Korean won, New Taiwan dollar, Chinese yuan, and euro.
- It mitigates FX risk using OTC derivatives—primarily foreign exchange forwards and options—aligned with the timing of underlying commitments.
- Hedging programs include cash flow hedges (to protect cash flows from sales/purchases), net investment hedges (to protect investments in foreign operations), and undesignated hedges (to offset economic currency risks on monetary balances and earnings), with notable use of average rate forwards to protect translated earnings in Japanese yen.
- Counterparty credit risk is managed by transacting with a diversified set of highly rated financial institutions; no collateral is required by either party, and no losses from counterparty defaults are expected.
- Sensitivity analysis: a 10% adverse FX move at December 31, 2021 could reduce the fair value of open FX derivatives and foreign-denominated debt by $0.7 billion (vs. $1.0 billion at December 31, 2020); for the Japanese yen specifically, the potential loss is $0.6 billion in 2021 (vs. $0.8 billion in 2020). These derivative losses are expected to largely offset gains on the hedged items and transactions.
- Item 8 refers to audited Consolidated Financial Statements and related notes located in Part IV, Item 15 of the Form 10-K.
- Item 9 reports no changes in, or disagreements with, accountants on accounting and financial disclosure.

nodes.title: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.heading: 1. Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.summary:
- Context: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements for Corning Incorporated, primarily covering Note 1 – Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, with cross-references to other notes.
- Organization and recent transactions:
  - Overview of Corning’s business lines (display glass, telecom networks, environmental substrates, life sciences, advanced optics, polysilicon).
  - 2020 HSG transaction: DuPont’s interest redeemed; Corning obtained 100% of HS LLC and 80.5% of HSO LLC; HSG results consolidated in “All Other.”
- Basis of presentation and consolidation:
  - U.S. GAAP; consolidation of majority-owned entities; equity method for significant influence (generally 20%–50%); fair value or cost-minus-impairment for other investments.
  - Elimination of intercompany accounts; prior-period reclassifications with no impact on results.
- Use of estimates:
  - Significant estimates in revenue recognition, restructuring, asset impairments, acquisitions, fair value of investments/equity interests, environmental/legal liabilities, income taxes and valuation allowances, pension/OPEB assumptions, and share-based compensation.
- Revenue recognition:
  - Predominantly point-in-time upon transfer of control; customer acceptance when required.
  - Measurement excludes sales/VAT; incidental contract costs expensed.
  - Variable consideration (returns, allowances, discounts) and warranty liabilities estimated.
  - Certain arrangements recognized over time using straight-line or input methods.
- Research and development:
  - Expensed as incurred; disclosed amounts for 2021–2019 ($0.8B, $1.0B, $0.8B).
- Foreign currency:
  - Functional currency determinations (most local; notable exception: a Taiwanese subsidiary uses JPY).
  - Transaction gains/losses in earnings; translation adjustments in accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI).
  - 2021 net translation gain; 2020 and 2019 transaction losses disclosed.
- Share-based compensation:
  - Options, restricted stock/units (time- and performance-based); grant-date fair value expensed over vesting.
  - Multiple-point Black-Scholes valuation model with assumptions for volatility, dividend yield, risk-free rate, expected term, and departure rates.
- Cash and cash equivalents; supplemental cash flow info:
  - Highly liquid investments with maturities ≤3 months; carrying value approximates fair value.
  - Disclosures of non-cash capex accruals and cash paid for interest (incl. capitalized) and income taxes for 2019–2021.
- Credit losses:
  - Allowance for doubtful accounts based on lifetime expected credit losses, historical write-offs, and expected default rates; specific reserves as needed; no significant off–balance sheet credit exposure.
- Environmental liabilities:
  - Accrued when probable and estimable; most likely cost approach; PRP sharing considered; minimum of range when no best estimate; insurance receivables recognized when virtually certain; acknowledgment of uncertainty.
- Inventories:
  - Lower of cost or net realizable value; FIFO.
- Property, plant, and equipment:
  - Recorded at cost; straight-line depreciation (buildings 10–40 years; equipment 2–20, with subcategories listed).
  - Precious metals components not depreciated; physical loss treated as depletion expense; metals held to support operations only.
- Leases:
  - Operating and finance leases recognized with ROU assets and liabilities (classification locations specified).
  - Operating lease expense straight-line; finance lease interest and amortization methods described.
  - Use of incremental borrowing rate when implicit rate unknown; renewals/terminations included when reasonably certain.
  - Practical expedient to combine lease and non-lease components; no significant lessor activity; no residual value guarantees; no primary beneficiary/VIE issues.
- Impairment of long-lived assets:
  - Trigger-based recoverability tests using undiscounted cash flows (including disposition); fair value via income approach (explicitly considers precious metals) when not recoverable; assessment at lowest cash-flow level; ongoing quarterly evaluation when indicators exist.
- Employee retirement plans:
  - Defined benefit pensions and postretirement health/life plans; key economic and demographic assumptions.
  - Pension cost components (ongoing vs. annual mark-to-market outside corridor; 10% corridor rule); remeasurement triggers.
  - Postretirement costs and recognition in AOCI with amortization.
- Income taxes:
  - Asset-liability method; deferred tax assets/liabilities for basis differences and carryforwards.
  - Uncertain tax positions recognized at the largest amount more likely than not to be sustained; adjustments as returns filed or new info arises; penalties/interest classification.
  - Discrete items recognized in period of occurrence; valuation allowances as needed.
  - Indefinite reinvestment assertion for specified categories of foreign earnings.
- Equity method and other investments:
  - Periodic impairment assessments; other-than-temporary impairments recognized to fair value.
  - Equity securities not under equity method at fair value through earnings or, when no readily determinable fair value, at cost minus impairment plus/minus observable price changes (measurement alternative).
- Fair value measurements:
  - Recurring (e.g., short-term investments, derivatives) and nonrecurring (e.g., impairments) fair value categories; principal/most advantageous market and market-participant assumptions considered.
- Derivatives and hedging:
  - FX forwards/options and interest rate swaps used for risk management.
  - All derivatives at fair value; cash flow and net investment hedge changes in AOCI with reclassification upon earnings impact; non-designated derivatives in earnings.
- New accounting standards:
  - Early adoption of ASU 2020-06 (convertible instruments and EPS if-converted method); no one-time adoption impact as of January 1, 2021.

nodes.title: Equity Method Investments
nodes.heading: Equity Method Investments
nodes.start_phrase:
Equity method investme
nts are reviewed for impairment on a periodic basis, or if an event occurs or circumstances change that indicate the carrying amount may  beimpaired.
nodes.summary:
- Section: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies (continued), focusing on equity investments, fair value measurements, derivatives, and new standards.
- Equity method investments: Assessed periodically for impairment based on performance and impairment indicators; fair value estimated via discounted cash flows or other methods when indicators exist; other-than-temporary impairments recorded in earnings with carrying value written down to fair value.
- Other equity securities: Those not consolidated and not under the equity method are measured at fair value with changes in net income; for investments without readily determinable fair values, the measurement alternative is used (cost less impairment adjusted for observable price changes). Related balances are disclosed in Note 3 (Investments).
- Fair value measurements: Recurring fair value for major financial assets and liabilities (e.g., short-term investments, other assets, derivatives); nonrecurring fair value applied upon impairment to long-lived assets, goodwill, asset retirement obligations, equity method investments, and certain other investments. Fair value defined as exit price; measurements consider the principal/most advantageous market and market participant assumptions including risk, transfer restrictions, and nonperformance risk.
- Derivative instruments: Use of FX forwards/options to hedge currency risk and interest rate swaps to manage benchmark rate exposure and fixed/floating debt mix; all derivatives recognized at fair value on the balance sheet. Hedge accounting: changes for cash flow hedges and net investment hedges recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and reclassified to the related income statement line when the hedged item affects earnings; non-designated derivatives’ fair value changes recognized in translated earnings contract gain (loss), net, and other income (expense), net.
- New accounting standards: Early adoption of ASU 2020-06 in Q1 2021, eliminating separate accounting for certain convertible instrument features (ASC 470-20), clarifying equity classification assessments (ASC 815-40), and requiring the if-converted method for diluted EPS for all convertibles, including potential share settlement when more dilutive (ASC 260). Adoption had no one-time impact as of January 1, 2021.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.heading: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.start_phrase:
Major categories of financial a
ssets and liabilities, including short-term investments, other assets and derivatives are measured at fair value on a recurring basis.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies (continued) covering equity method and other equity investments, fair value measurements, derivative instruments, and new accounting standards.

- Equity method investments:
  - Periodic impairment assessments based on performance and impairment indicators.
  - If indicators exist, fair value estimated via discounted cash flows or other appropriate methods.
  - Other-than-temporary impairments recognized in earnings with carrying value written down to fair value.

- Other equity securities:
  - Securities not consolidated and not accounted for under the equity method measured at fair value with changes in net income.
  - Measurement alternative applied for investments without readily determinable fair values: cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions.
  - Related balances disclosed in Note 3 (Investments).

- Fair value measurements:
  - Recurring fair value for major financial assets and liabilities (e.g., short-term investments, other assets, derivatives).
  - Nonrecurring fair value upon impairment for long-lived assets, goodwill, asset retirement obligations, equity method investments, and other investments lacking significant influence.
  - Fair value defined as exit price in the principal or most advantageous market; considers market participant assumptions including risk, transfer restrictions, and nonperformance risk.

- Derivative instruments:
  - Use of foreign exchange forwards and options to manage FX risk.
  - Interest rate swaps used to manage benchmark interest rate risk for forecasted debt issuance and fixed/floating mix.
  - All derivatives recorded at fair value on the balance sheet.
  - Hedge accounting: changes in fair value of cash flow hedges and net investment hedges recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCL) and reclassified to earnings when the hedged item affects earnings, in the corresponding income statement line (e.g., sales, cost of sales, other income/expense).
  - Non-designated derivatives’ fair value changes recognized in income (translated earnings contract gain/loss, net; other income/expense, net).

- New accounting standards:
  - Early adoption (Q1 2021) of ASU 2020-06:
    - Eliminates separate accounting for beneficial and cash conversion features under ASC 470-20.
    - Clarifies equity classification settlement assessment under ASC 815-40.
    - Requires if-converted method for diluted EPS for all convertible instruments, including potential share settlement for instruments that may be settled in cash or shares under ASC 260.
  - Adoption had no one-time impact as of January 1, 2021.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments
nodes.heading: Derivative Instruments
nodes.start_phrase:
The Company enters into a vari
ety of foreign exchange forward contracts and foreign exchange option contracts to manage the exposure to fluctuations in foreign exchangerates.
nodes.summary:
- Excerpt from the Summary of Significant Accounting Policies detailing investment, fair value, derivative, and new standards policies.
- Equity method investments: recurring impairment assessments; fair value determined via discounted cash flows or other methods when indicators exist; other-than-temporary impairments recorded in earnings. Non-equity-method equity securities measured at fair value through net income; use of the measurement alternative for investments without readily determinable fair values (cost less impairment plus/minus observable price changes), with related disclosures referenced to Note 3.
- Fair value measurements: definition and valuation framework based on principal/most advantageous market and market participant assumptions; recurring fair value for short-term investments, other assets, and derivatives; nonrecurring fair value for impaired long-lived assets, goodwill, asset retirement obligations, equity method and other non-influenceable investments.
- Derivative instruments: use of FX forwards/options and interest rate swaps to manage currency and interest rate risks; all derivatives recorded at fair value; hedge accounting for cash flow and net investment hedges with changes recognized in accumulated other comprehensive loss and reclassified to earnings when hedged items affect results; non-designated derivatives recognized in income (translated earnings contract gain/loss, net; other income/expense, net).
- New accounting standards: early adoption of ASU 2020-06 in Q1 2021, simplifying accounting for convertible instruments (eliminating separate BCF/CCF under ASC 470-20), clarifying equity classification under ASC 815-40, and requiring the if-converted method in diluted EPS under ASC 260; no one-time impact at adoption.

nodes.title: New Accounting Standards
nodes.heading: New Accounting Standards
nodes.start_phrase:
During the 
first  quarter of 2021,  Corning early adopted ASU 2020 -06.
nodes.summary:
- Covers Corning’s significant accounting policies and select results:
  - Equity method investments: periodic impairment reviews based on performance and impairment indicators; fair value measured via discounted cash flows or other methods when indicators exist; other-than-temporary impairments recorded in earnings with carrying amount written down to fair value. Equity securities not consolidated and not under the equity method are measured at fair value with changes in net income; for investments without readily determinable fair values, the measurement alternative (cost minus impairment plus/minus observable price changes) is used; related balances referenced to Note 3.
  - Fair value measurements: major financial assets and liabilities (e.g., short-term investments, other assets, derivatives) measured at fair value on a recurring basis; certain assets/liabilities (e.g., long-lived assets, goodwill, AROs, equity method investments, and non-influenced investments) measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis when impaired. Fair value defined as exit price in the principal or most advantageous market, incorporating market participant assumptions (risk, restrictions, non-performance).
  - Derivative instruments: use of FX forwards/options and interest rate swaps to manage currency and interest rate risks under corporate policies. All derivatives recorded at fair value; cash flow and net investment hedge changes recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and reclassified to earnings when the hedged item affects results; non-designated derivatives recognized in income (translated earnings contract gain/loss, net, and other income (expense), net).
  - New accounting standards: early adoption of ASU 2020-06 in Q1 2021 (simplifies accounting for convertibles, clarifies equity classification under ASC 815-40, requires if-converted method for diluted EPS under ASC 260); no one-time impact at adoption. ASU 2021-10 on government assistance disclosures effective Jan 1, 2022; not expected to be material. No other new standards expected to have a material impact as of Dec 31, 2021.
- Restructuring, impairment, and other charges/credits:
  - Summary of charges (in millions): 2021 total $110; 2020 total $827; 2019 total $439. Components include severance (2021 $(13), 2020 $148, 2019 $63), asset impairment (2020 $217), capacity realignment (2021 $46, 2020 $304, 2019 $312), and other charges/credits (2021 $77, 2020 $158, 2019 $64).
  - 2020 actions in response to uncertain global economic conditions: corporate-wide workforce reduction, asset disposals, accelerated depreciation tied to capacity realignment, and other exit activities to improve efficiency and cost structure.
  - Severance: 2020 program to realign Display Technologies capacity in Asia, optimize Optical Communications, and reduce corporate costs; charges of $148 million in 2020 and $63 million in 2019; payments substantially completed by Dec 31, 2021.
  - Asset impairment: in 2020, long-lived asset impairment and disposal loss ($217 million pre-tax) from discontinuing certain R&D programs within “All Other”; charge reflected substantially all carrying value, including an insignificant amount of goodwill.
  - Capacity realignment: 2020 primarily accelerated depreciation and asset disposals related to exiting certain facilities and other exit activities in Display Technologies and Specialty Materials; 2019 primarily accelerated depreciation related to exiting certain Display Technologies facilities.

nodes.summary: Section 11 presents detailed breakdowns of Other Assets and Other Liabilities as of December 31, 2021 and 2020, in millions, separated into current and non-current categories, with cross-references to related notes. Other assets include current derivative instruments and other current assets, and non-current items such as derivative instruments, South Korean tax deposits, operating lease assets (Note 7), investments (Note 3), and other non-current assets. It explains that CPM is appealing South Korean tax assessments and refund claims for 2010–2018, is required to deposit disputed amounts during the appeal, and management believes it is more likely than not to prevail (see Note 8). Other liabilities include current wages and employee benefits, income taxes, derivatives (Note 15), deferred revenue and customer deposits (Note 5), settlement liability (Note 4), share repurchase liability (Note 17), short-term leases (Note 7), and other current liabilities; and non-current defined benefit pension liabilities, derivatives, deferred revenue, settlement liability, customer deposits, share repurchase liability, deferred taxes, long-term leases, asbestos and other litigation, and other non-current liabilities. Reported totals: other current assets $1,026 (2021) vs $761 (2020); other non-current assets $2,056 vs $2,140; other current liabilities $3,139 vs $2,437; other non-current liabilities $5,192 vs $5,017. The section includes multiple cross-references to Notes 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 15, and 17.

nodes.summary:
- Section 11 (Other Assets and Other Liabilities) presents detailed schedules as of December 31, 2021 and 2020:
  - Other assets:
    - Current other assets totaled $1,026 million in 2021 (up from $761 million in 2020), driven by higher derivative instruments and other current assets.
    - Non-current other assets totaled $2,056 million in 2021 (slightly down from $2,140 million in 2020), including derivative instruments, South Korean tax deposits, operating lease right-of-use assets, investments, and other non-current assets.
    - South Korean tax deposits relate to CPM’s appeals of tax assessments and refund claims for 2010–2018; deposits are required during appeal, and the company believes it is more likely than not to prevail (see Note 8).
  - Other liabilities:
    - Current other liabilities were $3,139 million in 2021 (up from $2,437 million in 2020), including wages and employee benefits, income taxes, derivatives, deferred revenue, settlement liability, customer deposits, a new share repurchase liability, short-term leases, and other current items.
    - Non-current other liabilities were $5,192 million in 2021 (up from $5,017 million in 2020), including defined benefit pension liabilities (down vs. 2020), derivatives (down), deferred revenue, settlement liability, customer deposits, share repurchase liability (new), deferred taxes, long-term leases, asbestos and other litigation (down), and other non-current liabilities (up).

- Section 12 (Debt) outlines the company’s debt profile at December 31, 2021 and 2020:
  - Current portion of long-term debt was $55 million in 2021 (vs. $81 million in 2020); short-term borrowings were $75 million in 2020 and none in 2021.
  - Detailed long-term debt schedule includes multiple USD and yen-denominated debentures across maturities (2022–2079), medium-term notes, callable debentures, financing leases, and other borrowings.
  - Total long-term debt including current portion was $7.044 billion in 2021 (down from $7.897 billion in 2020); excluding current portion, $6.989 billion in 2021 (vs. $7.816 billion in 2020).
  - Fair value of long-term debt was $8.3 billion in 2021 and $9.4 billion in 2020, compared with book values of $7.0 billion and $7.8 billion, respectively; fair value measured using Level 2 inputs.
  - Foreign currency translation gains/losses on debt recognized in accumulated other comprehensive loss; cash proceeds from issuances shown in financing activities; interest payments in operating activities; bond redemptions in financing activities.
  - No outstanding commercial paper at year-end 2021 or 2020.
  - Revolving credit agreement: $1.5 billion unsecured multi-currency facility expiring August 15, 2023; no amounts outstanding at December 31, 2021.

- Discloses fair value of long-term debt of $8.3 billion at 2021 and $9.4 billion at 2020, exceeding book values; fair value measured using Level 2 inputs based on market yields.
- Explains accounting treatment: foreign currency translation gains/losses recognized in accumulated other comprehensive loss; cash proceeds from loans/debt issuances shown in financing activities; interest and bond redemptions shown in operating and financing activities, respectively.
- Notes no outstanding commercial paper at December 31, 2021 and 2020.
- Describes a $1.5 billion unsecured, multi-currency revolving credit facility expiring August 15, 2023, with no borrowings outstanding at December 31, 2021.
- Provides a debt maturity schedule as of December 31, 2021: $55 million (2022), $141 million (2023), $293 million (2024), $166 million (2025), $36 million (2026), and $6,353 million thereafter (excludes swap gains, discounts, and deferred expenses).
- Details 2021 debt actions: early redemptions of $375 million (2.9% due 2022) and $250 million (3.7% due 2023) via make-whole calls, with premiums and losses recognized in other income (expense), net; borrowings of approximately CNY 1,764 million (~$277 million) under unsecured variable-rate facilities; an undrawn JPY 25 billion (~$217 million) liquidity facility.
- Details 2020 debt actions: redemption of $100 million (7.0% due 2024) with make-whole premium and loss; establishment of JPY 25 billion three-year liquidity facility (undrawn at 2020 year-end); establishment of three unsecured CNY variable-rate facilities totaling CNY 2,345 million, with 2020 borrowings of CNY 1,691 million (~$243 million).
- Clarifies that CNY loan proceeds will be used for capital projects and not converted to USD; principal and interest to be repaid in CNY (or USD equivalent if CNY unavailable); these loans are obligations of subsidiary borrowers and are not guaranteed by other Corning entities.
- Notes a variable interest rate loan made in 2020 related to HSG’s change in control; associated third-party debt fully repaid by December 31, 2021.

nodes.summary:
- Section focuses on Employee Retirement Plans, specifically Defined Benefit Pension Plans and Postretirement (health and life insurance) benefits.

nodes.summary:

- Contribution activity:

nodes.title: Obligations and Funded Status

nodes.start_phrase:
The change in benefit oblig
ation and funded status of our defined benefit pension and post-retirement benefit plans are as follows (in millions):
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Employee Retirement Plans (defined benefit pension plans—domestic and international—and postretirement benefit plans), with detailed disclosures on obligations, plan assets, funded status, actuarial assumptions, expense components, and investment strategy for 2019–2021.

- Obligations and plan assets (2021 vs. 2020):
  - Domestic pension: benefit obligation $4,075m ($4,203m in 2020); plan assets $3,598m ($3,575m).
  - International pension: benefit obligation $736m ($778m); plan assets $584m ($598m).
  - Postretirement: benefit obligation $654m ($764m); plan assets $9m ($30m).
  - Rollforwards show service/interest costs, participant/employer contributions, actuarial gains/losses, benefits paid, and FX effects.

- Funded status at year-end:
  - Domestic pension: $(477)m deficit (improved from $(628)m in 2020).
  - International pension: $(152)m deficit (from $(180)m).
  - Postretirement: $(645)m deficit (from $(734)m).
  - Balance sheet presentation split between noncurrent assets/liabilities and current liabilities.
  - AOCI components at 2021 year-end: domestic pensions $294m (net actuarial loss and prior service cost), international $(2)m, postretirement $(42)m.

- Actuarial gains/losses and discount rates:
  - 2021: pension actuarial gain $124m from higher bond yields; discount rates up 37 bps (domestic) and 18 bps (international). Postretirement actuarial gain $105m; discount rate up 30 bps.
  - 2020: pension actuarial loss $358m and postretirement loss $58m from lower yields.
  - Accumulated benefit obligation (ABO) for pensions: $4.5b (2021) vs. $4.7b (2020).
  - Underfunded plan disclosure (2021): PBO $4,358m vs. assets $3,627m; ABO $4,110m vs. assets $3,627m.

- Net periodic benefit (income)/expense (2019–2021):
  - Components include service cost, interest cost, expected return, amortization of prior service and actuarial amounts, and recognition of actuarial losses.
  - 2021 totals: domestic pension income $(15)m; international pension expense $28m; postretirement expense $21m.
  - Special termination benefits noted in certain years.
  - Non-service cost components reported in other income (expense), net.

- Other comprehensive (loss) income activity (2019–2021):
  - Includes current-year actuarial gains/losses, recognitions, and prior service cost/credit amortization.
  - 2021 reflects significant actuarial gains for domestic pensions and postretirement.

- Discount rate methodology:
  - Based on a hypothetical yield curve from high-quality U.S. dollar corporate bonds (Moody’s, S&P, Fitch, DBRS), excluding outlier yields; uses spot-rate matching to determine the level discount rate.

- Mortality and actuarial assumptions:
  - Base tables: PRI‑2012 (white/blue collar); disabled mortality: PRI‑2012 with MP‑2020 improvements (updated in 2020; no change in 2021).
  - Company monitors Society of Actuaries updates.

- Weighted-average assumptions:
  - For obligations (2021 vs. prior years): discount rates, compensation increases, cash balance/employee contribution crediting rates presented for domestic/international pensions and postretirement.
  - Health care cost trend: 6.25% next year (6.50% in 2020), grading to 5% by 2027.

- Plan asset strategy:
  - Objective: sufficient returns to meet current/future obligations with liquidity.
  - Target allocation: ~40% equities (diversified by size and geography) and ~60% bonds (predominantly corporate), with long-duration fixed income to reduce interest rate sensitivity.

nodes.title: Hedging Activities

15.
 Hedging Activities

nodes.summary:
- Focus: Corning’s hedging activities and risk management related to foreign currency and commodity exposures.

- Instruments used: Over-the-counter foreign exchange forwards and options to mitigate income statement volatility from exchange rate movements.
- Counterparty risk management: Diversified, highly rated financial institutions; no collateral posting required; not expecting counterparty default losses; elected the Dodd-Frank end-user clearing exception.
- Designated cash flow hedges: FX forwards hedging forecasted sales and purchases; gross notional $780 million at Dec 31, 2021 ($1.1 billion at Dec 31, 2020); maturities 2022–2023; gains/losses deferred in accumulated other comprehensive loss; $47 million pre-tax gain expected to be reclassified to earnings within 12 months of Dec 31, 2021.
- Designated fair value hedges: 2021 leases of precious metals (maturities through 2025) with bifurcated embedded derivatives hedging changes in fair value of a precious metals pool; hedge results recognized in current earnings; time value component excluded and amortized; impact of excluded component not material; carrying amount of leased precious metals pool $107 million at Dec 31, 2021; cumulative fair value changes not material.
- Hedge effectiveness assessment: Initial via regression analysis or critical terms match; ongoing quarterly qualitative assessments.
- Undesignated hedges: FX forwards and options used economically (not hedge-accounted) to reduce functional currency volatility in subsidiaries’ monetary assets, liabilities, and net earnings.
- Translation risk management: Average-rate forwards and options to protect translated earnings for significant non-U.S. revenues/expenses, especially JPY exposure; maturities span 2022–2024.

- Ongoing SRA terms: SDC may offer up to 22 million additional shares to Corning in tranches during 2024–2027; if Corning declines and SDC sells on the open market, Corning owes a make-whole payment capped at 5% of the otherwise applicable repurchase proceeds. - Time-based restricted stock and RSUs:

nodes.summary:
- Section focus: Share-Based Compensation (continued), covering stock options, valuation assumptions, and restricted stock/RSU programs under Corning’s plans.
- Stock options:
  - Aggregate intrinsic value defined and measured using the December 31, 2021 closing price; about 7 million in-the-money options were exercisable at year-end 2021.
  - No option grants in 2021; weighted-average grant-date fair value of options granted was $3.67 (2020) and $8.78 (2019).
  - Total fair value of options vested: $16m (2021), $31m (2020), $10m (2019).
  - Stock option compensation cost: $9m (2021), $23m (2020), $13m (2019).
  - Unrecognized compensation cost at 12/31/2021: ~$10m, to be recognized over a weighted-average 1.3 years.
  - 2021 option exercise activity: proceeds $97m; realized tax benefit $15m; intrinsic value of options exercised $100m (vs. $99m in 2020 and $47m in 2019).
- Valuation methodology:
  - Multiple-point Black-Scholes model with blended volatility (short-term implied, expected-term recent volatility, 15-year historical), expected term based on historical exercise behavior and vesting, and risk-free rates from zero-coupon U.S. Treasuries for the expected term.
  - Key inputs:
    - 2020: expected/weighted-average volatility 32.9%; expected dividend 4.48%; risk-free 0.5%; expected term 7.4 years; pre-vesting departure rates: executives 0.6%, non-executives 2.5%.
    - 2019: expected/weighted-average volatility 29.5–29.9%; expected dividend 2.36–2.95%; risk-free 1.5–2.4%; expected term 7.4 years; executive pre-vesting departure 0.6%.
- Incentive Stock Plan:
  - Allows grants of restricted stock and RSUs (time- or performance-based), typically without cash consideration, at grant-date market price; vest over ~1–10 years; fair value equals grant-date price.
- Time-based restricted stock/RSUs:
  - Payable in shares upon vesting; expense recognized over vesting and adjusted for actual forfeitures.
  - Non-vested rollforward (thousands of shares; weighted-average grant-date fair value):
    - 12/31/2020: 12,943 at $22.87; Granted: 1,890 at $40.77; Vested: (3,774) at $23.40; Forfeited: (465) at $23.74; 12/31/2021: 10,594 at $25.83.
  - Unrecognized compensation cost at 12/31/2021: ~$117m, to be recognized over a weighted-average 2.1 years.
  - Total fair value of vested time-based awards: $88m (2021), $38m (2020), $33m (2019).
  - Compensation cost recognized: $94m (2021), $95m (2020), $43m (2019).
- Performance-based RSUs:
  - Earned upon achievement of specified targets; typically vest over three years; grant-date fair value assumes target payout; expense recognized over vesting, adjusted for forfeitures and updated for changes in expected performance outcomes during the performance period.

Notes that a controlling interest in HSG was obtained in Q3 2020 and consolidated in “All Other” from September 9, 2020.

- Section 19: Share‑Based Compensation (continued)
  - Details 2021 activity for performance‑based restricted stock units (PSUs): starting balance, grants, vesting, performance adjustments, forfeitures, and ending balance.

  - Compensation expense related to PSUs was about $79 million in 2021 and $81 million in 2020, largely driven by retirement‑eligible employees.

- Section 20: Reportable Segments
  - Defines five reportable segments and their activities:
    - Display Technologies (glass substrates for high‑performance displays)
    - Optical Communications (carrier and enterprise network components)
    - Specialty Materials (glass, glass ceramics, fluoride crystals with >150 formulations)
    - Environmental Technologies (ceramic substrates/filters for automotive and diesel)
    - Life Sciences (glass/plastic labware, equipment, media, serum, reagents for discovery/bioproduction)
  - “All Other” groups businesses below quantitative thresholds, including HSG, pharmaceutical technologies, auto glass, new product lines, development projects, and certain corporate investments.
  - Notes controlling interest in HSG obtained in Q3 2020; consolidated in “All Other” since September 9, 2020; cross‑reference to Note 4.
  - Segment reporting approach:
    - Prepared to align with internal reporting used by the CODM.
    - Excludes specified foreign currency fluctuations from segment sales and net income for certain segments (e.g., JPY/KRW/CNY/NTD for Display and Specialty; EUR/CNY for Environmental; EUR/CNY/JPY for Life Sciences).
    - Excludes certain corporate/non‑operational items from segment results (e.g., translated earnings contracts, acquisition costs, discrete tax items, litigation/legal matters, restructuring/impairments, acquisition adjustments, other non‑recurring items), though they are included in consolidated results.
    - Includes earnings of equity affiliates closely associated with segments.
    - Explains centralized functions and allocation methodologies; cautions that segment net income may not be comparable to other companies.

- Historical Segment Information (2019–2021 highlights)
  - 2021 totals: segment net sales $14.12B; net income $2.296B; depreciation $1.315B; RD&E $0.838B; capital expenditures $1.699B; segment assets $18.954B.
    - Largest 2021 sales by segment: Optical Communications $4.349B; Display Technologies $3.700B; Specialty Materials $2.008B; Environmental Technologies $1.586B; Life Sciences $1.234B; All Other $1.243B.
  - 2020 totals: segment net sales $11.452B; net income $1.628B; depreciation $1.215B; RD&E $0.754B; capital expenditures $0.928B; segment assets $19.022B.
  - 2019 totals: segment net sales $11.656B; net income $1.701B; depreciation $1.192B; RD&E $0.867B; capital expenditures $1.899B; segment assets $18.026B.
  - Trends noted: strong year‑over‑year growth in 2021 net sales across segments, with significant increase in “All Other” (reflecting HSG consolidation and other activities) and higher capital spending in 2021 versus 2020.
  - Footnote clarifications:
    - (1) Segment depreciation includes allocated corporate property depreciation.
    - (2) RD&E includes direct project spend identifiable to segments.
    - (3) Income tax provision reflects a 21% rate.
    - (4) Centralized administrative/staff functions allocated to segments; unallocated expenses included only in consolidated reconciliation.
    - (5) Segment assets comprise inventory, receivables, net PP&E, and associated equity companies; HSG assets included in 2021 and 2020.

nodes.summary: Exhibit 32 is the Sarbanes-Oxley Section 906 (18 U.S.C. §1350) certification by Corning Incorporated’s Chairman and CEO, Wendell P. Weeks, and Executive Vice President and CFO, R. Tony Tripeny, dated February 14, 2022. It certifies that the Company’s Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2021: (1) fully complies with Section 13(a) or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934; and (2) fairly presents, in all material respects, the Company’s financial condition and results of operations. The exhibit includes their signatures and a copyright notice.
